title: Sum of an Array

concept.title: The accumulator pattern
body: Many problems are solved by walking through the data once and keeping a running answer. That running answer is called an **accumulator**. For a sum, the accumulator starts at `0` and each number is added to it.
Visiting every element exactly once takes time proportional to the number of elements. We write that as **O(n)**, and it is the baseline to compare faster or slower ideas against.

Watch the size of the answer. A 32-bit integer holds values up to about 2.1 billion. Adding many large numbers can pass that limit and silently wrap around. In C++ use `long long` (64-bit) when the total can be large. Python integers have no limit.

statement: You are given a list of integers. Print the sum of all of them.
inputFormat: The first line contains one integer `n`, the number of integers.
The second line contains `n` integers separated by spaces.
outputFormat: Print one integer: the sum of the `n` numbers.
hints: Start with a variable `total = 0` and visit every number once.
How large can the total get? Up to 50000 numbers of size 10^9 add up to 5 * 10^13. That is more than a 32-bit integer can hold.
In C++ read the numbers into `long long` and keep `total` as `long long` (in Java use `long`). Python needs no special care.

starter.python:
# Read n, then n integers, and print their sum.
n = int(input())
numbers = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: Keep one variable, `total`, that starts at 0. Go through the numbers one by one and add each to `total`. When the loop ends, `total` holds the answer.
The numbers can add up to 10^14, so the C++ version uses `long long` for both `total` and the numbers it reads.
solution.complexity: Time O(n), extra space O(1) in C++ (O(n) in the Python version, which stores the list).

code.python:
n = int(input())
numbers = list(map(int, input().split()))

total = 0
for x in numbers:
    total += x
print(total)
